newsitem.title: INDIA: ASEAN may admit Burma in July, Thai official says.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN may admit Burma in July, Thai official says.

text.p: Thailand's deputy foreign minister said on Thursday that he expected Burma, Cambodia and Laos to win admission into the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) this year, possibly in July.
Pitak Intravitayanunt told Reuters in the Indian capital that he saw no obstacle to Burma joining the seven-nation ASEAN grouping despite concern over its human rights record.
"We see hope that we will go to receive the three countries this year," Intravitayanunt said on the sidelines of a meeting with Indian businessmen.

Foreign ministers of the ASEAN nations -- Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- will meet in Kuala Lumpur on Saturday to decide when to admit its final three members.
ASEAN said last year it would admit all three together.
Malaysia, this year's ASEAN chairman, has been pressing for Burma, Laos and Cambodia to be inducted at ASEAN's annual ministerial meeting scheduled for July 24-25 in Kuala Lumpur.
Another proposal would admit the three at an informal ASEAN summit in December, to which Japan, South Korea and China have also been invited.
"Technically, they are ready. We don't see snags or anything to delay the admission of the three countries," the Thai official said.
Asked if a decision would be taken before or at an ASEAN ministerial meeting set for July, he said: "We don't have the definite timetable, but July will be a possible date."
Intravitayanunt was asked if Burma's human rights record would stand in the way of entry into ASEAN.
"For us, we look at the long perspective. We don't look at it just in one angle. All three are our neighbours with which we enjoy good relations," he said.
Political instability in Cambodia and a feud between leaders of its coalition government have raised doubts over whether it could pass the legislation required to join ASEAN before the July meeting.
Meanwhile, ASEAN is being pressured by the United States to delay Burma's entry because of its human rights record.

Aung San Suu Kyi, who is leading a pro-democracy movement against Burma's military rulers, said in a video interview released on Thursday that Burma's leaders could become "even more obdurate and oppressive than ever" if the country gained entry into the ASEAN.
